comparator.academicYear: Current curriculum for prospective cohorts after 2026, checked 2026-09-28
comparator.sourceNotes: The official current curriculum accounts for 180 EC. Year 1 is a fixed 60-EC foundation of eight 7.5-EC courses. The generic target names no track, so the first-listed Migratie en mondiale ontwikkeling track is selected by neutral official order: four 7.5-EC track courses (30 EC). Two first-listed SGPL electives supply 15 EC of major choice. The programme states that students take two SGPL electives in the major and otherwise use profiling space; the remaining 45 EC of profiling space is kept genuinely open. Year 3 closes with three 5-EC research-and-context courses and a 15-EC bachelor thesis. The resulting pathway totals 60 EC foundation + 45 EC selected major + 45 EC profiling + 30 EC final research semester = 180 EC.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The closest programme integrates the target’s social-spatial, environmental and mixed-method core. The first two evidenced track directions after that core—migration/global development and inclusive cities—produce feasible, materially different UCR curricula. Planning sustainable cities and innovative sustainable regions are also coherent but production stops at the three-alternative maximum.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both examine how communities and institutions respond to environmental risks in delta landscapes.
Both analyse institutional choices and contested spatial-environmental interventions, though the Utrecht course is a historical planning foundation.
Both use geospatial data to analyse and visualise place-based change; UCR concentrates on earth observation.
UCR has no dedicated Planning for Open Cities course.
UCR has no dedicated transport-geography course.
Both analyse urban social relations and institutions; Utrecht adds a dedicated geographical and planning frame.
Both examine disciplinary assumptions, institutions and normative frames, though Utrecht focuses on geography and planning.
Both supply theoretical frameworks for migration and global relations; UCR is international-relations theory rather than migration geography.
Both examine global connections and uneven development; UCR uses historical empire as its main lens.
No selected UCR course reproduces the full migration-and-global-development themes course.
No selected UCR course reproduces the track-specific Trans-Mob Lab practice atelier.
No selected UCR course provides Utrecht’s integrated geography, fieldwork and European-border component.
Both develop advanced quantitative analysis for independent social-spatial research.
Both introduce quantitative and qualitative research design; Utrecht applies it specifically to socio-spatial safety questions.
Both are applied mixed-method, place-based research projects, with different substantive settings.
Both develop qualitative research design, interviewing, observation and analysis.
No selected UCR course reproduces this separately credited geography-and-planning context component.
No scheduled UCR course is a bachelor thesis; UCR’s standard optional independent-research element is shown alongside it.
The comparator’s 45-EC profiling space is genuinely open; UCR flexibility is distributed across the complete 180-EC programme.

notes.text: Utrecht supplies a continuous disciplinary sequence in social geography and planning, including spatial data, track-specific mixed-method research, practice work and a bachelor thesis. UCR combines strong sociology, politics, economics, sustainability, environmental science, data and research courses but does not offer the same full geography-and-planning or professional planning sequence. The UCR alternatives are related academic paths rather than equivalent credentials.
